topic_summary: Aggregation, normalization, correlation, and alerting — the four jobs every SIEM shares.

flashcards.front: Name the four core functions of a SIEM.
flashcards.back: 1) Log aggregation, 2) normalization, 3) correlation, 4) alerting (with optional response/case management).
Translating raw logs from many vendors into a common schema (CIM/ECS/etc.) so downstream queries don't care about the source format.

flashcards.front: What is correlation in a SIEM?
flashcards.back: Combining multiple events across sources/time into a single higher-fidelity signal (e.g., failed-logins + new-process + outbound-c2 = lateral-movement alert).

flashcards.front: Give one trade-off of high-cardinality fields in a SIEM.
flashcards.back: Great for investigation pivots, but expensive to index and aggregate — drives storage/license cost up.

questions.stem: Which SIEM function is most directly responsible for reducing analyst toil from vendor-specific log formats?
questions.explanation: Normalization maps vendor fields to a common schema, so analysts write queries against one model.

questions.stem: You combine three lower-fidelity rules into a single higher-fidelity alert. What SIEM concept is this?
questions.explanation: Correlation links multiple events into a single signal — the textbook 'failed-login + new-process + c2-beacon' chain.

questions.stem: True or false: a SIEM with no normalization can still do effective cross-source correlation.
questions.explanation: Without normalization the SIEM cannot reliably join fields across vendors — correlation collapses to per-source patterns.
